blocks.text: A plastic bottle cap costs a fraction of a cent to make, yet the steel mould that forms it can cost as much as a house. Both facts are true because the mould cost is paid once and then spread across hundreds of millions of caps. How a manufacturer divides cost into things paid once and things paid per part decides which process is economic at which volume.

blocks.markdown: The cost of making a part can be split into four main elements. **Material cost** is the raw material actually consumed (including scrap and waste). **Labour cost** is the direct operator time multiplied by the labour rate. **Tooling cost** covers dies, moulds, patterns, jigs and fixtures, often paid before the first part and spread over the production run. **Overhead** is everything else that keeps the factory running: machine depreciation, power, maintenance, supervision, floor space, and is usually charged as a machine-hour rate or as a percentage of direct labour.

blocks.title: Fixed and variable cost
blocks.text: A **fixed cost** does not change with the number of parts made in a run (tooling, programming, setup). A **variable cost** is incurred for every part (material, direct labour, energy). The total cost of making $N$ parts is $C(N)=F+vN$, and the unit cost is $c=F/N+v$, where $F$ is the fixed cost (currency) and $v$ the variable cost per part (currency/part).

blocks.caption: Cost elements of a manufactured part

blocks.title: Unit cost breakdown
blocks.prompt: A part has 0.8 kg of material at 3.00 currency units per kg. The cycle takes 90 s, operator labour is 30 units per hour, the machine overhead rate is 40 units per hour, and tooling of 12 000 units is spread over 20 000 parts. Find the unit cost and each share. All figures are illustrative, not real cost data; overhead is allocated per part as the hourly rate times the cycle time.
blocks.answer: The unit cost is 4.75 units: material 51 percent, labour 16 percent, tooling 13 percent and overhead 21 percent.

blocks.markdown: Two routes to the same part usually trade fixed against variable cost. A flexible route (such as CNC machining from bar) has low fixed cost and high variable cost; a dedicated route (such as casting or forging with a die) has high fixed cost and low variable cost. At low volume the flexible route is cheaper, at high volume the dedicated route is. The **break-even quantity** $Q^*$ is the volume at which both routes cost the same.

blocks.caption: Break-even quantity between process A (low fixed, high variable) and process B (high fixed, low variable)

blocks.title: Break-even between machining and casting
blocks.prompt: Process A, CNC machining from bar, has fixed cost 1500 units and variable cost 14.00 units/part. Process B, casting plus finishing, has fixed cost 9000 units and variable cost 6.50 units/part. Find the break-even quantity and say which is cheaper at 400 and at 5000 parts.
blocks.answer: Break-even is 1000 parts. Machining is cheaper below it (400 parts) and casting is cheaper above it (5000 parts).

blocks.markdown: This explains why high tooling costs favour high-volume production. The tooling charge per part is $T/N$. For a die costing 60 000 units it is 600 units per part at 100 parts, 60 at 1000 parts and only 0.60 at 100 000 parts. Only at high volume does the tooling share fall below the savings the dedicated process brings in material and labour. Tooling also wears out: a die that lasts 100 000 parts needs a second die for a run of 150 000, so the fixed cost rises in steps.

blocks.title: Amortisation
blocks.text: Tooling cost per part is $T/N$. A high-tooling process pays only if volume is large enough that $T/N$ becomes smaller than the saving per part $v_A-v_B$, which is exactly the break-even condition $N>T/(v_A-v_B)$ when the other fixed cost is ignored.

blocks.title: Break-even assumes known volume
blocks.text: A break-even calculation is only as good as the volume forecast. If demand is uncertain, a low-fixed-cost process lowers the risk of an unrecovered tooling investment even if its unit cost is higher. Also check that both processes meet the quality requirements.

points: Unit cost splits into material, labour, tooling and overhead; $c=F/N+v$.
Break-even quantity is $Q^*=(F_B-F_A)/(v_A-v_B)$; below it the low-fixed-cost process wins, above it the low-variable-cost process wins.
High tooling cost is spread over all parts, so it is justified only by high volume.
Tooling wear and uncertain demand must be considered in the decision.

questions.stem: Which of these is a fixed cost for a production run of stamped brackets?

distractorRationale.a: Material is consumed in proportion to the number of parts.
distractorRationale.c: Direct labour per part scales with the number of parts.
distractorRationale.d: Energy per stroke scales with the number of strokes.

questions.explanation: A die is bought once and its cost does not depend on how many parts it makes within its life. Material, direct labour and energy all rise in proportion to output, so they are variable costs.

questions.stem: A part has material cost 3.20, direct labour 1.10, overhead 0.90 (all currency units per part), and a tooling cost of 25 000 units spread over 50 000 parts. Calculate the unit cost in currency units.
questions.explanation: Tooling per part is $25000/50000=0.50$. The unit cost is the sum $3.20+1.10+0.50+0.90=5.70$ units.

questions.stem: Process A has fixed cost 4000 units and variable cost 9.00 units/part. Process B has fixed cost 22 000 units and variable cost 3.00 units/part. Calculate the break-even quantity in parts.
questions.explanation: Setting $4000+9Q=22000+3Q$ gives $6Q=18000$, so $Q^*=3000$ parts. Below this A is cheaper; above it B is cheaper.

questions.stem: For the two processes in the break-even calculation (A: low fixed cost, high variable cost; B: high fixed cost, low variable cost), which is cheaper at a quantity below the break-even?

options.text: They cost the same at all quantities

distractorRationale.a: Process B's large fixed cost has not yet been spread over enough parts, so it is more expensive below break-even.
distractorRationale.b: They cost the same only at the break-even quantity.
distractorRationale.c: Material cost is part of the variable cost but the choice depends on the full cost comparison.

questions.explanation: At low volumes the fixed cost per part $F/N$ dominates, so the low-fixed-cost process wins. Past the break-even quantity the lower variable cost of B outweighs its higher fixed cost.

questions.stem: A factory allocates the cost of the building, lighting and supervisors to jobs in proportion to the machine hours used. Into which cost element does this fall?

distractorRationale.b: Direct material is the raw material that becomes part of the product.
distractorRationale.c: Direct labour is the operator time spent working on the part.
distractorRationale.d: Tooling is the dies, moulds and fixtures made for the part.

questions.explanation: Costs of running the factory that cannot be traced to a single part are overhead, and are usually charged through a machine-hour or labour-hour rate. They are added to material, labour and tooling to give the unit cost.

questions.stem: Why do high tooling costs favour high-volume production?

options.text: High volume reduces the tooling wear to zero
Tooling cost is paid by the customer
The tooling cost per part falls in proportion to $1/N$ as the run gets larger
High volume increases the material cost per part

questions.correctOptionText: The tooling cost per part falls in proportion to $1/N$ as the run gets larger

distractorRationale.a: Wear increases with use, it does not vanish.
distractorRationale.b: The tooling is part of the producer's cost and is recovered through price, not paid separately.
distractorRationale.d: Material cost per part is basically unchanged by volume.

questions.explanation: Because the tooling charge is $T/N$ per part, doubling the run halves the tooling share. At high volume it becomes negligible compared with the savings of the dedicated process.

questions.stem: A forming die costs 85 000 units and lasts for 100 000 parts, after which a new die of the same price is needed. The variable cost is 1.40 units/part. For an order of 250 000 parts, how many dies are needed and what is the average unit cost? Give the unit cost in currency units.
questions.explanation: Tooling needed is $\lceil250000/100000\rceil=3$ dies, so $T=3\times85000=255000$. The unit cost is $255000/250000+1.40=2.42$ units, which is more than if tooling cost were counted once.

questions.stem: Process A has fixed cost 2000 units and variable cost 12 units/part. Process B has fixed cost 10 000 units and variable cost 4 units/part, giving a break-even of 1000 parts. If B's tooling cost rises by 4000 units, what is the new break-even quantity?

distractorRationale.a: This is the old break-even; the extra fixed cost moves it upward.
distractorRationale.b: This would need the fixed-cost gap to reach 16 000 units, but the gap is only 12 000.
distractorRationale.c: This halves the old figure; more tooling cost can only raise the break-even.

questions.explanation: The new break-even is $(14000-2000)/(12-4)=1500$ parts, up from $1000$. Because the fixed-cost gap grew by 4000 and each part saves 8 units, the volume needed to recover it rises by 500.

questions.stem: A new component will be made as 500 pieces in the first year and possibly 50 000 a year thereafter. A forging die costs 60 000 units and saves 5 units per part in material and machining compared with machining from bar. Explain, with numbers, why the forging route may or may not be justified in year one and later.
markingGuide: Tooling per part is $T/N$: 60 000/500 = 120 units per part in year one
Saving of 5 units per part is far below 120 units, so forging is not justified at 500 parts
At 50 000 parts tooling per part is 1.2 units, well below the 5 unit saving
Mentions demand uncertainty, tool life, or staged investment
questions.explanation: The break-even volume is 60 000/5 = 12 000 parts, so the die is not justified by 500 parts but pays back quickly at 50 000. Uncertain demand suggests waiting for higher volume or machining until volume is proven.

questions.stem: Describe how the unit cost of a turned part is built up from material, labour, tooling and overhead, and say which of these elements are fixed and which are variable. Then explain how the break-even quantity between two processes is found and what factors could invalidate it.
markingGuide: Material: mass times price (including scrap) - variable
Labour: cycle time times rate - variable
Tooling: cost over run size - fixed amortised
Overhead: fixed factory cost, allocated per part through a machine-hour rate (rate times cycle time) or a percentage of labour
Limitations: uncertain volume, tool life steps, quality, lead time, setup frequency
questions.explanation: Unit cost is the sum of per-part terms (material, labour) plus a fixed term spread over the run (tooling); overhead is a fixed cost that is allocated to each part through an hourly rate, so it enters the unit cost as a per-part term. Break-even equates total cost for the two routes, but depends on a reliable volume and on both routes meeting the quality specification.
